lessons.title: Fixed Income: FDs, G-Secs and Corporate Bonds as the Risk Anchor

children.text: A fractional ownership platform advertises a 9% yield on a pre-leased office floor in Pune. A P2P app shows 12%. An unlisted NCD from a regional NBFC offers 13%. On their own, each number sounds attractive. But none of them means anything until you ask one question: what could I earn with almost no risk at all? In India, the answer comes from the Government of India's own bonds. Subtract that, and the 9% office yield shrinks to a much smaller reward for tenant risk, vacancy, platform risk and a hard exit. This lesson turns fixed income into the ruler you measure every yield-based alternative against.

body.text: Fixed income is the ruler, not just an asset. Before you admire any yield, subtract what the Government of India will pay you for taking no credit risk. What is left is your real reward for everything that can go wrong.

children.text: India's Risk-Free Starting Line

markDefs.definition: The return on an investment with effectively no chance of default, used as the base for judging every riskier return. In India, it is usually taken as the yield on government securities of a similar maturity.

children.text: The
risk-free rate

in India is the yield on Government of India securities: treasury bills for under a year, and G-Secs for longer periods. The government borrows in its own currency, so the chance of it failing to repay a rupee bond is treated as effectively zero. Retail investors can buy these directly through RBI Retail Direct, or through stock brokers such as Zerodha.
Two other anchors sit very close to the starting line for most households:
Bank FDs up to the insured limit.
Deposits are protected by DICGC insurance up to a fixed amount per depositor, per bank.
Small savings schemes.
PPF, NSC and the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme are backed by the government, with rates reset each quarter.

body.label: DICGC deposit insurance limit
body.context: Covers principal and interest together. Money above this limit in a single bank carries that bank's credit risk.

body.label: RBI Retail Direct
body.description: RBI's platform for individuals to open a Retail Direct Gilt account and buy government securities and treasury bills directly.

children.text: The Yield Ladder: Every Step Up Is a Risk Taken

markDefs.definition: The extra yield a riskier bond or loan pays over a government security of similar maturity, as compensation mainly for the chance of default.

children.text: Starting from government securities, each rung up the ladder pays a higher yield because you are taking more risk. The gap between any rung and the government yield is the
credit spread

body.title: An illustrative Indian yield ladder (% a year, indicative only)

body.latex: \text{Spread} = \text{Yield on the investment} - \text{G-Sec yield of similar maturity}
body.caption: The spread is what you are paid for credit risk, illiquidity and everything else that can go wrong

body.text: Yields change with interest rates, so the exact numbers on the ladder move every year. The spreads between rungs are more stable, and they are what you should remember. A government bond yielding 6.5% and a P2P loan yielding 12% means you are being offered 5.5 percentage points for lending unsecured money to individuals you have never met.

children.text: Fixed Income Is an Anchor, Not a Guarantee
Only the bottom rungs are close to risk-free. Indian investors have met all four fixed income risks in the last decade:

body.caption: The four fixed income risks, with Indian examples

cells: Interest rate risk
Bond prices fall when rates rise, hurting long-duration bonds and funds
RBI raised the repo rate from 4% to 6.5% between May 2022 and February 2023, and longer-duration bond funds had weak returns
Credit risk
The issuer stops paying, even if it was highly rated
IL&FS carried top ratings shortly before defaulting in 2018
Liquidity risk
You cannot get your money when you need it
In 2019, RBI capped withdrawals at PMC Bank after irregularities surfaced, freezing depositors' savings
Inflation risk
Interest does not keep up with rising prices, so purchasing power shrinks
A low FD rate during a high-inflation year can mean a negative real return

body.title: When a bank bond turned out not to be an FD: Yes Bank AT1 bonds

markDefs.definition: Additional Tier 1 bonds: perpetual bonds issued by banks to count towards their capital. Their terms allow them to be written down if the bank gets into serious trouble.

children.text: In March 2020, as part of Yes Bank's reconstruction, its
AT1 bonds

, worth about ₹8,400 crore, were written off. Depositors were protected, but bondholders lost their money. Many of those bondholders were individual investors who had been sold the bonds as a safe, higher-yield alternative to FDs.
The lesson: a bank's name on an instrument does not make it a deposit. The extra yield on AT1 bonds was payment for exactly the risk that came true. Always check where you rank if things go wrong.
What You Actually Keep: Real, Post-Tax Returns

Interest from FDs, bonds, NCDs and P2P loans is taxed at your income tax slab rate. Gains on debt mutual fund units bought from April 2023 onwards are also taxed at slab rates. For investors in higher brackets, this changes the comparison dramatically.

body.caption: A quick approximation, good enough for comparing options
A 7% FD at different tax rates, with 5% inflation (illustrative, ignoring cess)

children.text: For someone in the 30% bracket, a 7% FD roughly preserves purchasing power and little more. That is the honest job of fixed income: stability and a known cash flow, not wealth creation. It also explains why high-yield alternatives tempt so many investors, and why the tax treatment of those alternatives, covered in Chapter 5, matters so much.

body.title: Real return on a corporate bond
body.prompt: An investor in the 20% tax bracket buys an AA-rated corporate bond yielding 7.5%. Inflation is 5%. Using the approximation above, what is the real post-tax return, in percent? Ignore cess.
body.explanation: 7.5% × (1 − 0.20) = 6.0% after tax. 6.0% − 5% inflation = about 1.0% real. The investor is taking AA credit risk for a real return of about one percentage point a year.

children.text: How the Anchor Behaves in a Crisis

When growth collapses, RBI usually cuts rates. It cut the repo rate from 9% in October 2008 to 4.75% by April 2009, and to 4% by May 2020. Falling rates push up the prices of existing high-quality bonds, so government securities have tended to cushion portfolios exactly when equities crashed. Lower-rated credit behaved very differently: in those same periods, it became harder to sell and more likely to default.

body.title: True anchors vs yield products dressed as fixed income

columns.label: Behaves like an anchor
points: Bank FDs within the DICGC limit
PPF, NSC and the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme
AAA-rated PSU bonds and high-quality gilt or corporate bond funds

columns.label: Looks like fixed income, behaves like risk
points: Private credit and real estate debt deals

children.text: Using the Anchor: The Spread Test

For any yield-based alternative, find the closest traditional instrument with a similar level of risk and an exit you could actually use. The difference is the premium for the alternative's extra risks and lock-in. Then ask whether that premium is big enough.

body.caption: The spread test applied (illustrative yields, before costs and expected losses)

cells: P2P loans to individuals
A-rated NBFC NCD
2 points, for unsecured borrowers and no secondary market
Fractional pre-leased office
AAA PSU bond
2 points, for single-tenant, vacancy and exit risk
Private credit AIF (net estimate)
AA corporate bond
1.5 points, for a multi-year lock-in and concentration
Unlisted developer NCD
10-year G-Sec
8.5 points, a sign the market sees serious default risk

body.text: A very large spread is not a bargain. It is the market telling you something. When an instrument offers 8 or 9 percentage points over a G-Sec, investors who have studied the borrower have concluded there is a real chance of losing money. Assume they know something you do not.

body.title: Pick the right ruler
body.question: You are evaluating a 5-year real estate debt deal offering 13%. Which is the most appropriate risk-free starting point to measure its spread from?
options: The yield on a Government of India security maturing in about 5 years
The Nifty 50's long-run return of about 12%
body.explanation: Spreads should be measured against a government security of similar maturity. A savings rate is too short-term and not a market yield, the repo rate is an overnight policy rate, and the Nifty is an equity return, not a risk-free rate.

body.title: Name the gap
body.textWithBlank: The extra yield a corporate bond pays over a government security of the same maturity is called the credit ___.
body.explanation: The credit spread is the market's price for the chance that the issuer does not pay. It widens sharply in crises, which is when lower-rated bonds lose value fastest.

body.title: The Iyers' retirement income
body.scenario: Mr and Mrs Iyer, both 63, live in Coimbatore and have ₹80 lakh in savings. They need steady income for the next 20 years. A relative suggests putting all ₹80 lakh into unlisted NCDs issued by a local NBFC, paying 12% monthly. Their bank manager points out that they could each invest in the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme, which pays 8.2%, and keep the rest in bank FDs spread across banks.
body.prompt: Apply the ideas from this lesson. How should the Iyers think about the 12% NCD against the government-backed options?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Start from the anchor. SCSS is government-backed. Each of them can invest up to ₹30 lakh, so ₹60 lakh can go in at 8.2%, and the remaining ₹20 lakh can sit in FDs within DICGC limits across banks.

2. Measure the spread. 12% minus 8.2% is about 3.8 percentage points, for lending to a single small NBFC with no government backing. The unlisted NCD also has no easy exit.

3. Think about what the spread pays for: default risk of one NBFC, no deposit insurance, liquidity risk if they need money for medical costs, and concentration of their entire retirement in one issuer. IL&FS and the Yes Bank AT1 write-off show that even well-known names can fail.

4. Think about the downside. The extra 3.8 points on ₹80 lakh is about ₹3 lakh a year before tax. A default could cost them a large part of the ₹80 lakh that has to last 20 years.

5. Conclusion: for retirees relying on this money, fixed income should be an anchor. Government-backed and insured options should form the core. If they want any higher-yield exposure, it should be a small slice, diversified across issuers and understood as risk capital.

points: Government of India securities set India's risk-free rate, and every yield-based alternative should be measured against a G-Sec of similar maturity.
Each step up the yield ladder, from G-Secs to AAA and AA bonds to NCDs, P2P and private credit, pays a spread for more risk.
Fixed income is an anchor, not a guarantee: interest rate, credit, liquidity and inflation risks have all hit Indian investors in the last decade.
Interest is taxed at slab rates, so a 7% FD in the 30% bracket earns roughly zero after 5% inflation.
High-quality government bonds have tended to cushion portfolios in crises, while lower-rated credit has behaved more like equity.
Use the spread test: a small spread may not pay for the alternative's extra risks, and a very large one is a warning, not a bargain.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation to buy or avoid any security, deposit or scheme. Yields shown are illustrative and change with interest rates. Small savings scheme rates, deposit insurance limits and tax rules can change. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a tax professional before making decisions.
